Montréal adopte une motion amendée sur G: Montréal adopts amended motion on Gaza after divided debate
Montréal adopts an amended motion on Gaza after a divided debate over the City’s role in the conflict and its local repercussions.
La motion déposée par Projet Montréal po: The motion tabled by Projet Montréal, asking the City of Montréal to recognize the genocide in Gaza and suspend its institutional ties with Israel, was ultimately not adopted in its original form. After significant amendments proposed by Soraya Martinez Ferrada’s administration, the opposition voted against the changes, saying the text had been “heavily modified.” The amendments were nonetheless accepted by a vote of 38 to 22, and the amended motion was then adopted by a vote of 54 to 6.
Le débat a opposé deux conceptions du rô: The debate pitted two conceptions of the City’s role against each other when facing an international conflict with local repercussions. For the mayor, Montréal must acknowledge the gravity of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, uphold international law and protect civilian populations, but city council must not become a place where “international conflicts are brought in.” For the opposition, on the contrary, silence is not an option. Its leader, Ericka Alneus, said residents expected elected officials to “call things by their name” and that, despite the changes made to the motion, the fact that Montréal held this debate was already a signal.
Avant le dépôt de la motion, la conseill: Before the motion was tabled, councillor Nathalie Goulet invoked Montréal’s tradition as a “pacifist city,” recalling in particular the stance the City took against apartheid in South Africa. “Are we still capable of that courage?” she asked.
La mairesse Soraya Martinez Ferrada a re: Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada acknowledged the gravity of civilian suffering in Gaza, but challenged city council’s legitimacy to legally characterize the situation as genocide. “City council is not an international court of justice,” she said. In her view, Montréal’s role is rather to act within the scope of its direct responsibilities: safety, prevention of hate acts, intercultural dialogue and social cohesion. She also allowed members of her team to vote freely, acknowledging the existence of “different and legitimate convictions” within the majority.
La version de la motion qui a finalement: The version of the motion that was ultimately adopted no longer includes the two main demands of the original version: the City’s recognition of a genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, and the suspension of institutional and commercial ties with the State of Israel, its institutions and its municipalities. The new text instead affirms city council’s solidarity with the Palestinian people and the civilian victims of the hostilities, reiterates the importance of fighting antisemitism and Islamophobia, and reaffirms Montréal’s commitment to international law and international humanitarian law.
Toutefois, la motion adoptée appuie expl: However, the adopted motion explicitly supports the work of judicial bodies and international organizations mandated to examine allegations of violations of international law in Gaza, notably the ongoing proceedings before the International Court of Justice concerning the application of the Genocide Convention. It also asks the governments of Canada and Quebec to show “greater leadership,” notably by respecting international law and imposing sanctions on the parties and individuals responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law and human rights.
L’opposition a refusé les amendements. P: The opposition rejected the amendments. For Ericka Alneus, the motion was indeed “heavily modified,” but the debate itself was important. “Montréal had this debate,” she said, stressing that international conflicts have very real repercussions on Montréal communities.
Nathalie Goulet s’est dite déçue par la: Nathalie Goulet said she was disappointed by the administration’s position and its refusal to recognize the genocide in Gaza. She pointed in particular to Montréal precedents on human rights, including the severing of ties with apartheid South Africa.
Pour elle, l’argument du vivre-ensemble: For her, the argument of living together cannot justify inaction. “Montréal’s living together [...] cannot mean living together with apartheid and genocide,” she said.
La question de l’antisémitisme a égaleme: The issue of antisemitism was also raised during the debate. Earlier in the meeting, the administration had passed a motion aimed at fighting antisemitism. Projet Montréal had voted against it, while explicitly condemning the attacks targeting Jewish schools and a synagogue. Its opposition concerned the political scope of the text and its potential effects on council’s freedom of debate.
À propos de Gaza, les élus de Projet Mon: On Gaza, Projet Montréal councillors also insisted on a distinction they consider essential: criticizing the decisions of the Israeli government is not the same as targeting Jewish people. Olivier Demers had stressed the need to distinguish “criticism of a state, its policies, its military actions” from “hatred toward Jewish people.”
<strong>Une mobilisation devant l’hôtel: A rally in front of city hall
Le débat s’est déroulé après la mobilisa: The debate took place after a rally of about a hundred people in front of city hall. At noon, in a persistent rain, activists, artists, union members and human rights defenders took turns at the microphone to call for the adoption of the original motion.
Le rassemblement était notamment organis: The rally was organized by Montréal Anti-Apartheid and the Ligue des droits et libertés, among others. The motion had the support of more than 130 organizations, more than 1,100 Quebec artists and nearly 1,500 citizens. For Zev Saltiel, a representative of Montréal Anti-Apartheid and a member of Independent Jewish Voices Montréal, the expected vote should not be regarded as a mere symbolic gesture. “The decision you are about to make today is not a symbolic decision,” he told elected officials.
References to 1987 were everywhere. Actor and author Nathalie Doumard recalled the artistic mobilization in favour of severing ties with South African apartheid. “In 1987, Montréal cut all ties with apartheid in South Africa. I am here today to ask Madam Mayor Martinez Ferrada to do the same for Palestine,” she said.
Diane Lamoureux, présidente de la Ligue: Diane Lamoureux, president of the Ligue des droits et libertés, for her part rejected the idea that Montréal could sidestep the debate by citing its municipal jurisdiction. “Montréal’s elected officials cannot dodge the issue by saying it is not up to cities to take a position,” she said. In her view, “the City, whether it likes it or not, is already involved,” notably through its own institutional and commercial relationships.
Bertrand Guibord, président du Conseil c: Bertrand Guibord, president of the CSN’s Conseil central du Montréal métropolitain, pointed out that the conflict also directly affects Montréal families. “We cannot turn our heads away from the genocide unfolding before our eyes,” he said. Finally, Rama Al Malah, of the Palestinian Youth Movement, placed the mobilization within a broader international movement.
À la fin du rassemblement, elle retenait: At the end of the rally, what stood out most to her was its size despite the rain: “We haven’t seen a turnout like this in a little while.”
Pour les organisations mobilisées, le vo: For the mobilized organizations, Monday’s vote therefore does not close the issue. Rather, it marks a new stage in a campaign that has been demanding for several years that Montréal turn its stances on human rights into institutional action.
